title: Population Genetics II: Genetic Drift & Selection
objectives: Differentiate genetic drift from natural selection
Calculate effects of population bottlenecks and founder effects
Analyze selection patterns through fitness coefficients
Apply concepts to human genetic disorders

genetic_drift.title: Genetic Drift Mechanisms
genetic_drift.content:
Founder Effect
• Example: Ellis-van Creveld in Amish
• Mechanism: Few founders → ↑recessive alleles
• Impact: 1:200 vs 1:60,000 general population
Population Bottleneck
• Example: Cheetahs (0.1% genetic diversity)
• Human Analog: Pingelapese color blindness

selection_types.title: Selection Patterns
selection_types.content:
TypeFitness PatternHuman Example
Directional↑One extreme phenotypeLactase persistence
Balancing↑HeterozygotesSickle cell trait
Negative↓Deleterious allelesTay-Sachs in non-Jewish

mathematical_models.title: Quantitative Analysis
mathematical_models.content:
Selection Coefficient (s)
s = 1 - w
• w = relative fitness
• sTT = 1 for lethal recessive
Drift Magnitude
Ne = (4NmNf)/(Nm + Nf)
• Effective population size
• Human Ne ≈ 10,000 historically

evolutionary_medicine.title: Disease Susceptibility
evolutionary_medicine.content:
• Thrifty Gene Hypothesis: Diabetes risk from feast-famine adaptation
  • Hypertension: Salt retention advantage in hot climates
  • Autoimmunity: Ancient pathogen defense → modern self-reactivity

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why do founder populations show higher recessive disease rates?

Genetic drift disproportionately affects small populations - rare alleles can become common by chance (e.g., Finnish disease heritage).

How does balancing selection maintain two harmful alleles?

Heterozygote advantage (e.g., sickle trait against malaria) outweighs homozygote disadvantage at population level.

Why are lethal dominant alleles rarer than recessive?

Strong negative selection removes them each generation (s=1), while recessives 'hide' in heterozygotes (e.g., Huntington's vs Tay-Sachs).
